stem: A client with acute ischemic stroke has not yet had swallowing safety assessed. Which nursing action is most appropriate before giving oral food, fluids, or medications?

options.A: Complete an approved bedside dysphagia screen before oral intake; if the screen is abnormal, restrict oral intake and arrange further swallowing evaluation according to the stroke protocol.
options.B: Offer a small amount of water first because formal screening has little role in identifying aspiration risk after stroke.
options.C: Skip dysphagia screening if the client speaks clearly because swallowing impairment occurs only when aphasia is present.
options.D: Assume that passing a bedside screen guarantees that aspiration and hospital-acquired pneumonia cannot occur.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline states that bedside dysphagia screening before oral intake has inherent clinical logic because it can identify patients at risk, guide additional definitive swallowing assessment, and inform nutritional management. Observational data suggest screening may reduce pneumonia, but the guideline also emphasizes that screening does not prevent every episode of aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia and that no single screening method has been proven superior. B initiates oral intake before screening. C falsely links dysphagia only to aphasia. D overstates the protective value of a passed screen.
educational_objective: Before oral intake after acute stroke, use the facility's validated dysphagia-screening process to identify swallowing risk and trigger further evaluation when needed while recognizing that screening reduces risk but does not guarantee prevention of aspiration or pneumonia.
source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
source_locator: Section 5.2 Dysphagia — Synopsis: bedside screening may help prevent aspiration and pneumonia through early identification of at-risk patients, but screening/formal evaluation/oral-intake restrictions do not prevent all aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 1–3: there is inherent logic in screening for dysphagia before oral intake; screening may reduce pneumonia in observational studies, guide additional definitive testing, and aid nutritional management; no specific screening method has proven superiority.
source_claim_supported: Post-stroke dysphagia screening before oral intake can identify patients at risk and guide further swallowing/nutritional evaluation; it may reduce pneumonia risk but does not guarantee prevention of aspiration or pneumonia and no single screening method is universally superior.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: perform focused screening and assessments that identify aspiration risk and complications before initiating care activities that could increase harm.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — post-stroke dysphagia screening before oral intake
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw rationale into a nursing safety action using the current 2026 AHA/ASA dysphagia guidance and corrected the blueprint from Safety & Infection Prevention and Control to Reduction of Risk Potential. The final item avoids claiming screening eliminates aspiration pneumonia and avoids mandating one specific screening instrument.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against Section 5.2 of the January 2026 AHA/ASA AIS guideline.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reflects screening-before-oral-intake and follow-up evaluation. B creates oral exposure before screening. C falsely makes dysphagia dependent on aphasia. D turns a risk-reduction screen into a guarantee.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; screen before oral intake and escalate abnormal findings.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; initial oral intake should not be used as a substitute for the screening process.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; post-stroke dysphagia can occur without aphasia.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; screening cannot prevent all aspiration or pneumonia.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The item intentionally says 'approved bedside dysphagia screen' rather than naming a specific instrument because the guideline finds insufficient evidence to prefer one method universally.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address swallowing-risk management before oral intake.
audit_findings.blueprint: Screening for aspiration-related risk fits Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked screening evidence strength, aspiration/pneumonia limitations, aphasia independence, and lack of a universally superior tool. The final answer does not claim a guaranteed outcome and no second defensible answer remained.
